title: What is Covenant?
summary: In the Bible, covenant language describes relationships shaped by promises and, in some passages, stated obligations. The details vary: Genesis 9 emphasizes God's promise to Noah and every living creature, while Exodus 24 depicts Israel affirming covenant words and sharing a meal.
historical_context: The cited passages present covenant in distinct narrative settings: God's promise after the flood (Genesis 9), the call and promise to Abraham (Genesis 12), Israel's covenant ceremony (Exodus 24), Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, and Jesus' words over the cup in Luke 22. This sequence follows the texts' presentation; it is not a reconstruction of the dates or social origins of each practice.
canonical_context: The selected passages show both continuity and difference. Genesis 9 emphasizes a promise extending to all living creatures; Genesis 12 centers on God's promise to Abraham; Exodus 24 includes covenant words, a blood rite, and a shared meal; Jeremiah 31 promises renewed relationship and instruction; and Luke 22 and Hebrews 8 connect covenant language with Jesus and the promised new covenant. Reading them together reveals a developing biblical storyline, while each passage retains its own participants, actions, and emphasis.
literary_context: Covenant is shown through scenes and speeches rather than one all-purpose definition. In Genesis 9 God speaks a promise and gives a sign; in Exodus 24 the people hear and affirm the covenant words before a meal; Jeremiah 31 presents a future promise; and Luke 22 places covenant language in Jesus' final meal with his disciples. Noticing who speaks, what is promised, and whether obligations or signs are named helps readers avoid treating every covenant passage as identical.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect relationship with promise, but they do not all describe the same arrangement. Genesis 9 stresses God's commitment; Exodus 24 includes Israel's response to covenant words; Jeremiah 31 speaks of forgiveness and instruction written on the heart; and Hebrews 8 interprets that promise in relation to Jesus. These differences help explain why later biblical writers can draw on earlier covenant texts while still describing a new covenant.
canonical_role: What is Covenant? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not assume every covenant passage assigns the same obligations to every participant. Compare what is promised, who responds, and which signs or actions the text names in Genesis 9, Exodus 24, and Jeremiah 31.

Read the covenants together while preserving their distinct scenes and terms: Genesis 9, Genesis 12, Exodus 24, and Jeremiah 31 emphasize different promises and responses, while Luke 22 and Hebrews 8 interpret covenant language in relation to Jesus.
